sections.html:
Pulaski County is Arkansas's most populous, with 399,125 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 404,611 for 2025, and Little Rock is both its seat and the state capital. Inside its borders are North Little Rock, Jacksonville, Maumelle, Sherwood, Alexander, Cammack Village and Wrightsville. One assessor and one treasurer serve all of them, but neighborhoods, school districts and city rules differ a great deal from one to the next.

Jacksonville left the Pulaski County Special School District after voters approved the separation on September 16, 2014, and the Jacksonville North Pulaski School District began on July 1, 2016. The special district still serves other parts of the county, so confirm the district for your address before you describe the house to a buyer.

A Pulaski County bill passes through three offices. The assessor sets the value, the clerk keeps the appeals calendar and the treasurer takes the payment.

OfficeLocationPhoneUse it for
Assessor201 S. Broadway, Suite 310, Little Rock501-340-6170Value and property record questions
County Clerk401 W. Markham St., Suite 100501-340-8500 (Real Estate department 501-340-8433)Equalization Board hearings
County TreasurerLittle Rock501-340-8345Payments and payoff figures

The county runs a four year reappraisal cycle ending in 2026, handled by its own staff across 177,110 parcels. Taxable value across the county was about $9.73 billion in 2024, and the total millage listed is 58.81. Under Act 139 of 2023, every Arkansas county will be on a four year reappraisal cycle by 2028.

Assessment notices go out in July, and the clerk's office begins scheduling Equalization Board appointments around the same time. The last day to schedule a hearing is the third Monday in August. After the board's regular meetings, which run through the end of September, you can take an appeal to County Court by the second Monday in October.

The board holds a first meeting in early August to organize and receive the real and personal assessment rolls. It may meet in special session starting in October if needed, and when the ratio of assessed value to market value falls short a special session can run into the third Monday in November. Because the dates shift slightly, confirm them with the clerk each year.

Arrive with evidence. The owner carries the burden of showing the value is wrong, and comparable sales, photographs of defects and repair estimates are the usual proof.

sections.h2: Caps, homestead credit and the senior freeze
sections.html:
Arkansas caps the yearly increase in taxable value at 5 percent for a homestead and 10 percent for other real property. Under Amendment 79, the caps hold until the property reaches full assessed value. They do not apply to new construction, newly discovered property or substantial improvements, meaning renovations that add 25 percent or more to value.

Landlords feel the 10 percent cap on non-homestead property most. A rental valued well under market at the last reappraisal keeps climbing by that much every year until the gap closes, which a buyer of an investment house will notice.

Living in the house earns you the homestead credit: up to $500 a year, rising to up to $600 on 2026 bills. Age 65 or older, or a disability, can also freeze taxable value. That protection is yours alone. Whoever buys from you starts at the current value and may pay more than you did.

sections.h2: Preparing for a call with the Assessor
sections.html:
Most value questions can be settled without a hearing. Before you call 501-340-6170, pull up your property record and read it line by line. Check the square footage, the number of bathrooms, whether a garage or outbuilding is listed that no longer exists, and the condition rating. A wrong detail is the easiest kind of error to fix.

Then gather two or three recent sales of houses close to yours in size and age. Photographs of a failing roof, a cracked slab or water damage back up a request for a lower value. If you have a repair estimate, bring it too.

Write down who you spoke with and when. If the call does not settle things, the clerk's office is the next stop for a hearing, and the notes help you explain what you already tried.

Arkansas collects property tax in the year after the assessment, so a Pulaski County closing often falls while a bill is unpaid or has not been issued yet. Ask the closing agent how the bill will be divided between seller and buyer and get the figure in writing.

Back taxes are the usual complication. If the property is behind, ask the Treasurer for a full payoff, including penalty and fees, so the title company can settle it from the sale proceeds. The state also charges a transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on transactions over $100, under Ark. Code 26-60-101 and following, and the state sells the transfer stamps.

Little Rock's neighborhoods include The Heights, Hillcrest and Pleasant Valley, and the Quapaw Quarter holds three National Register historic districts. Other listed districts are Capitol-Main, Central High School and MacArthur Park. A house inside one of them can give a buyer pause, so find out early whether yours is.

The humid climate shows up as moisture in roofs, crawl spaces and bathroom floors, and a buyer who orders an inspection will look at each. Older Little Rock and North Little Rock houses with moisture damage can be hard to sell through a retail listing.

• An inherited house with several years of unpaid tax and nobody living in it.
  • A rental with tenants in place and a reappraisal notice showing a higher value.
  • A house in a listed historic district that a buyer may hesitate over.
  • An owner relocating on short notice for a job at a hospital, bank or the air base.

A direct sale to a buyer who purchases as is takes repairs and showings out of the timeline. The price still reflects condition, so compare any written offer with the tax and lien payoff on your statement to see the net.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or an inherited house
sections.html:
Tenants and heirs add steps. If a tenant lives in the house, tell the title company and share the lease so the buyer sees the term and rent. If several heirs own it, everyone has to sign the deed, and an out-of-town heir can often sign by mail or through a notary.

An inherited house that nobody lives in tends to collect unpaid tax. Ask the Treasurer for the full balance early and decide whether you will pay it first or let the closing do it. The longer it stays unpaid, the more penalty and fees ride along on the payoff.

Once an offer is accepted, the title company searches the record and asks the Treasurer for the payoff. Gather the last tax statement, the deed and any notices from the assessor. If you rent the house out, have the lease ready so the buyer sees it.

At the table you sign the deed. The title company pays the Treasurer from proceeds, buys the transfer stamps, files the deed with the clerk and hands you the balance. With no lender involved, a cash sale can close faster, though it can still depend on how clean the title search is.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Pulaski County property assessment?
faqs.a: Call the Assessor at 501-340-6170, or visit 201 S. Broadway, Suite 310 in Little Rock. The County Clerk at 501-340-8500 schedules Equalization Board hearings.

faqs.q: What is the last day to appeal a Pulaski County assessment?
faqs.a: The third Monday in August is the last day to schedule an Equalization Board hearing. A further appeal to County Court is due by the second Monday in October.

faqs.q: Is Pulaski County on a four year reappraisal cycle?
faqs.a: Yes, the cycle ends in 2026. County staff do the work themselves across 177,110 parcels.

faqs.q: Does my senior tax freeze go to the buyer if I sell?
faqs.a: No. It stays with you. The buyer's taxable value resets at the next assessment.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Pulaski County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Back taxes are normally paid out of the proceeds. Phone the Treasurer at 501-340-8345 for a payoff figure before you sign.
